title: The vendored f2c layer declares integer as long int, which is a memory error on any LP64 build
body: **What we found.** The twelve vendored `f2c.h` copies declare `typedef long int integer`. On Windows LLP64 that is 4 bytes and is right. On Linux and any other LP64 target it is 8, so the translated routines read and write as 8 byte integers the 4 byte `int` objects their own callers pass. The same harness and the same input on two trees that differ by one typedef. The control dies in the sanitizer; the branch finishes. **Why it matters.** This is not a portability inconvenience. AddressSanitizer reports a stack buffer overflow READ of size 8 at `genmmd.c:88` and a WRITE of size 8 at `dpotrf.c:95`, both through `Sparse_factor_spd` at `src/flatten/sparse_solve.c:192`. Anything that reaches that solver on an LP64 build is exposed, not only the tools we were timing. **That the control can fail.** A clean sanitizer run proves nothing unless the same harness on the same input is still dirty without the change. Two of our three attempts at a control were worthless and we say so: our own tree already carried the change and came back clean, and bare `main` does not configure on Linux at all. The control that counts is `main` plus the three Linux changes of our other pull request plus #14, the smallest tree that builds here, and it still declares the eight byte integer. **The numbers**, one row per tree, same harness and same input, one change between them: | tree | sanitizer lines naming `genmmd`, `dpotrf`, a stack overflow | the run | |---|---|---| | control, `main` + three Linux changes + #14 | 3, and 2 naming the overflow | exit 1, did not finish | | the same tree with the width change | 0, 0, 0 | exit 0, `scroll_whole: OK (total 27.1s)` | The change is 12 files and 71 lines added and 71 removed, every one a typedef of six types; a diff filtered for lines that are not a typedef returns nothing. Nothing under `src/` moves. `ctest` passes 3 of 3 on the branch. We have not run the wider shipped suite on it, and we have not audited every use of `integer` in the vendored sources: we found two sites, fixed the declaration they share, and the symptom went. **How to check it yourself.** Build the smallest tree that compiles here with `-fsanitize=address`, run `scroll_whole` on one cube, then change the six typedefs in the twelve `f2c.h` copies and run it again on the same input. --- `deps/taucs/external/src/f2c.h` line 10, and the eleven copies of it under `deps/clapack`, all say typedef long int integer; On Windows LLP64 `long int` is 4 bytes and this is exactly right. On Linux and on any other LP64 target it is 8, and the translated routines then read and write as 8 byte integers the 4 byte `int` objects their own callers pass. `deps/taucs/src/taucs_ccs_order.c` declares and passes `int n, maxint, delta, nofsub` and `int*` arrays at its lines 273 and 410. AddressSanitizer, both through `Sparse_factor_spd` at `src/flatten/sparse_solve.c:192`: - **stack buffer overflow READ of size 8** at `deps/taucs/external/src/genmmd.c:88` - **WRITE of size 8** at `deps/clapack/SRC/dpotrf.c:95` A write of the wrong width through a sparse solver is undefined behaviour that happens to have worked. It is not a portability inconvenience and it is not confined to the tools we were timing: anything that reaches `Sparse_factor_spd` on an LP64 build is exposed. ## What we changed to get past it In our own tree, the twelve vendored `f2c.h` copies, `long int` to `int` for `integer`, `uinteger`, `logical`, `flag`, `ftnlen` and `ftnint`, which is the width the translated code was written against. **Nothing under `src/` had to change.** With that, AddressSanitizer is clean on the same run and the window completed. We have this on a branch. **Say the word and we will open it as a pull request**; we have not, because twelve changed vendored files is the kind of change a maintainer may well prefer to make his own way, and because #14's author reports that fixes have disappeared from `main` and from history, which suggests the public tree is periodically exported from a private one. If that is so, a vendored change is better made on your side than merged from ours. ## The state of that branch, stated so nobody has to ask It is cut from `main`, it changes 12 files and 71 lines, every one of them a typedef of the six types above, and nothing else in any header moves: a diff filtered for lines that are not a typedef returns nothing. **It is verified now, and the control is the part worth reading.** A sanitizer run that comes back clean proves nothing unless the same harness, on the same input, is still dirty without the change. Ours took three attempts to get a control that could fail. The first was our own working tree, which already carried the change, so it came back clean in 27.1 s and proved nothing. The second was bare `main`, which does not configure on Linux at all. The third is `main` plus the three Linux changes of our other pull request plus **#14**, which is the smallest tree that builds here, and it still carries `typedef long int integer`: | tree, same harness and same input | result | |---|---| | control, without the width change | **exit 1**, AddressSanitizer reports a stack buffer overflow at `genmmd`, 3 lines naming it and 2 naming the overflow | | the same tree, with the width change | **exit 0**, `scroll_whole: OK (total 27.1s)`, zero lines naming `genmmd`, `dpotrf` or a stack buffer overflow | One change between the two trees. On that branch the build is clean and **`ctest` passes 3 of 3**. Every figure of this section, and the shape of the check itself, is in `runs/rev1/growth-gate-cost/evidence/sanitizer-f2c.csv`, one row per quantity with what it was measured against: twelve rows, and each one agrees with what the verification requires, including the row that says the control still declares the eight byte integer. ## What we are not claiming We have not audited every use of `integer` in the vendored sources. We found two sites with a sanitizer, fixed the declaration they share, and the symptom went away on the run that had shown it. There may be places where the 8 byte width was load bearing and our change is wrong for them. What we have run on the branch is the CMake build and `ctest`, which passes 3 of 3; **the wider shipped suite we have not run on the branch**, only the three CMake tests, and the section above says exactly what was measured and against which control.
